solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Best access to the penthouse? (3-6)

blocks.note: of the highest class or standard
the last set of stairs up to the highest floor

annotation.surface: An estate agent boasting about the grand way up to a luxury flat.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words for the second half: the TOP FLIGHT of stairs is literally how you reach the top floor. The question mark flags that playful reading.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjective sense: top-flight work is first-rate, and the stair meaning is a pun on the same words.

entries.clue: English flag is placed on Scottish island (5)

indicatorNotes.is placed on: in a down clue the first piece is placed on top of, so above, the second

blocks.note: to flag = to tire, lose energy

annotation.surface: An English flag planted on a Scottish island, a small border provocation.
annotation.walkthrough: "Flag" looks like a banner, but it is the verb meaning to grow weary.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tiree is one island of the Inner Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast.

entries.clue: Celebrate Luton? Put a rosy gloss on it (5,3,4,3)

annotation.definition2: Luton? Put a rosy gloss on it

blocks.note: to go out on a wild night of celebration

blocks.clueFragment: Luton? Put a rosy gloss on it
blocks.note: Luton is a town; coat it in red

annotation.surface: A cheeky suggestion for brightening up an unglamorous English town.
annotation.walkthrough: Luton, a town north of London, stands in for "the town", and the second half takes the idiom literally: gloss is paint, rosy is red.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for a riotous night out, which the Luton half reads word by word as decorating.

entries.clue: Place where “posh” has replaced a mode of speech (8)

indicatorNotes.has replaced: one letter has taken another's spot: U goes in where the A of LOCATION was

blocks.note: U = upper-class; it replaces the A

annotation.surface: A spot where a plummy accent has taken over the local way of talking.
annotation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s split of "U" and "non-U" words, those the posh did and did not use.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a locution is a particular form of expression or phrasing.

entries.clue: Sacks of grit (4)

blocks.note: an army that sacks a town strips it bare

annotation.surface: Bags full of grit, like those put out on icy roads.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sacks" looks like a noun (bags) but is a verb: to plunder a building and empty it out.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the verb for stripping a building's insides, and the noun for courage.

entries.clue: Disaster as artist in new trick messed up (5,5)

indicatorNotes.messed up: something messed up has been thrown into disorder, so these letters are put out of order

blocks.note: RA goes in with these letters

annotation.surface: A painter's attempt at a new trick goes horribly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: RA is the usual crossword artist. Mix RA with NEW TRICK to get the ten letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative use: a literal rail crash has become slang for any chaotic failure or person in crisis.

entries.clue: Game suddenly moves quickly (5)

blocks.note: the pub game of throwing at a board

annotation.surface: A game that has abruptly sped up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, but it splits after "Game": a noun, then a verb phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the name of the pub game, and the verb for a sudden quick movement.

entries.clue: Topping of dark rum on the Parisian’s piece of cake (6)

indicatorNotes.Topping of: the topping sits on top, and in a down entry the top letter is the first
indicatorNotes.the Parisian’s: a Parisian speaks French, so the Parisian's "the" is LE

annotation.surface: A slice of cake finished with a dark rum topping, French style.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rum" is the old adjective (odd), not the drink. A doddle is British slang for an easy task.
annotation.definitionFit: Two slang phrases for the same thing: British doddle and piece of cake both mean an easy job.

entries.clue: Jumper, sensible to trap moderate warmth inside (4,11)

indicatorNotes.to trap: a trap closes around its catch, so MATURE closes around TEMPER

blocks.note: to temper = to moderate; goes after the M

annotation.surface: A sensible woolly jumper, made to keep a gentle warmth in.
annotation.walkthrough: "Jumper" is the sweater in the surface but a kangaroo in the wordplay, and "moderate warmth" is split: moderate is wordplay, warmth starts the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the standard comfortable warmth of an indoor room.

entries.clue: American poet has penned something to hold up (9)

indicatorNotes.has penned: to pen is to shut in, as sheep in a pen, so the poet shuts US inside

blocks.note: standard abbreviation; goes after the S

annotation.surface: An American poet has written something worth holding up as an example.
annotation.walkthrough: "American poet" wants to be one person; American is US and the poet is Spender. "Penned" looks like writing, which a poet does.
annotation.definitionFit: A functional definition: a suspender is a strap that holds up stockings or socks.

entries.clue: God wearing two sorts of animal pelt (4,4,3,4)

blocks.note: dressed in, as in "in a coat"

annotation.surface: A deity dressed in a coat made from two kinds of animal fur.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pelt" looks like a fur, which fits the animals, but it is the verb for rain beating down.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to rain cats and dogs is to pour, just as rain pelts down.

entries.clue: Being ancient, it yields hoards (6)

indicatorNotes.hoards: to hoard is to keep something stored away, and these words keep the answer stored inside them

annotation.surface: An ancient creature giving up its stash of treasure, like a dragon.
annotation.walkthrough: "Being" looks like a verb starting a phrase, but it is the noun: a creature or thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: a being is something that exists in its own right.

entries.clue: Strip of hot jerky mum’s brother eats (8)

indicatorNotes.jerky: moving in jerks and jolts, so the letters are shaken out of order
indicatorNotes.eats: what is eaten ends up inside, so UNCLE takes the letters in

annotation.surface: An uncle munching a strip of spicy dried meat.
annotation.walkthrough: "Jerky" is dried meat in the surface, and "strip" of meat goes with it; both are misdirection.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to strip someone is to take their clothes off.

entries.clue: Without beer regularly, teams end resentful (10)

indicatorNotes.Without: in its old sense of outside, so EMED stands outside BITTER
indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: tEaMs EnD, the even letters; split around BITTER

annotation.surface: A team finishes the season sour because the beer ran out.
annotation.walkthrough: "Regularly" belongs to "teams end", not to "beer", which it follows. Bitter is a hoppy English ale.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone embittered has been made bitter and resentful.

entries.clue: Teacher’s slimy speech about church backing ladies? (10)

indicatorNotes.about: around, so SMARM goes around the rest
indicatorNotes.backing: going backwards, so LOO is read from right to left

annotation.surface: A teacher's oily sermon about the church supporting women.
annotation.walkthrough: "The ladies" is a British name for the women's toilet, the loo. "Teacher's" reads as Teacher is.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a schoolmarm is a teacher, usually a prim, old-fashioned one.

entries.clue: Ultimately this medication left unexpected consequences (9)

annotation.definitionNote: Spillover is a mass noun, so it can stand for a plural like consequences, much as damage stands for many harms.

indicatorNotes.Ultimately: in the end, so the last letter

annotation.surface: A drug that turned out to have side effects nobody expected.
annotation.walkthrough: "Left" is not the direction or L here, but over, as in food left over.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: spillover is the knock-on effect of something beyond where it was aimed.

entries.clue: Surrounded by a thousand in support (4)

indicatorNotes.in: inside, so a thousand goes inside the word for support

annotation.surface: A thousand people encircling someone to back them up.
annotation.walkthrough: "A" in the clue is only the article: the answer's A comes from AID.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: amid means in the middle of, with things all around.

entries.clue: Beautiful rug, so oil damaged (8)

indicatorNotes.damaged: something damaged is broken up, so these letters are broken and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A lovely carpet ruined by an oil spill.
annotation.walkthrough: "Beautiful rug" reads as one phrase, but the definition stops after the first word.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: glorious is a stronger word for beautiful, as in a glorious view.

entries.clue: One not dressed for digging? (4)

indicatorNotes.dressed: to dress is to arrange, as a shop window is dressed, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone who has turned up to a dig not in work clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: "Digging" is slang for liking, and the question mark flags the slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Both slang: if you are digging something you are into it, keen on it.

entries.clue: Taxing period from a scary life at sea (6,4)

indicatorNotes.at sea: to be at sea is to be confused, so the letters are confused

annotation.surface: A sailor's gruelling stint in a frightening life at sea.
annotation.walkthrough: "Taxing" looks like tiring, but read it literally: the period over which tax is charged.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading of taxing: the fiscal year is the twelve months over which taxes are assessed.

entries.clue: Filmmaker’s arrogance casting the lead (6)

indicatorNotes.casting the lead: to cast off is to throw away, and the lead is the first letter, so H is thrown away

annotation.surface: A director whose arrogance shows in how the star is cast.
annotation.walkthrough: "Casting the lead" sounds like choosing a film's star, which fits the director, but here casting means throwing off.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialised sense: an auteur is a film director whose personal style marks the whole film.

entries.clue: City businessmen carrying women’s cases (8)

indicatorNotes.carrying: what is carried is held within, so the city and businessmen hold W between them

annotation.surface: Men in suits in the City of London lugging women's briefcases.
annotation.walkthrough: "Cases" looks like luggage but means legal cases. "City businessmen" suggests London's financial district; here City is LA.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a lawsuit is a case brought in a court of law.

entries.clue: Mission taking soldiers back to African capital (6)

indicatorNotes.back: going back means going backwards, so RE is read from right to left

annotation.surface: A military mission returning troops to an African capital city.
annotation.walkthrough: "Capital" means money, not a city: the rand is South Africa's currency. RE are the Royal Engineers.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an errand is a small mission you are sent on.

entries.clue: Poet new in 1265? (5)

indicatorNotes.in: inside, so N is placed inside the date

blocks.note: 1265 is an example of a date, flagged by the question mark

annotation.surface: Who was the new poet on the scene in 1265?
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is also true: Dante was born in 1265, so the poet really was new then.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy.

entries.clue: Fruit roly-poly has 1p off (4)

indicatorNotes.has 1p off: a price with 1p off is a penny cheaper; read 1p as one letter P, which comes off

annotation.surface: A roly-poly pudding marked down by a penny.
annotation.walkthrough: Roly-poly is a British rolled suet pudding, which fits the fruit, but here it means plump.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the plum is one kind of stone fruit.

entries.clue: Spine of clever album torn unfortunately (9,6)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters come out wrong way round

annotation.surface: The spine of a clever album, or book, sadly torn.
annotation.walkthrough: "Spine" looks like the back of an album cover; it is the body's backbone.
annotation.definitionFit: The anatomical term: the vertebral column is the stack of vertebrae we call the spine.

entries.clue: Technology that can track both ways (5)

indicatorNotes.both ways: a word that works both ways reads the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: five letters that read the same in each direction

annotation.surface: A system that follows targets coming and going.
annotation.walkthrough: The track here is the line of letters: RADAR reads identically in either direction, while the surface means tracking aircraft.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: radar is a technology for tracking objects by bouncing radio waves off them.

entries.clue: Block a play in part of Syria’s capital (9)

blocks.note: a scene is one part of a play

annotation.surface: A theatre production held up in one district of Damascus.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail "of Syria's capital", an adjective phrase: Damascene describes things from Damascus.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective of place: Damascene means of or from Damascus, Syria's capital.
